title: Stonewire Software x Redwood — SIEM-ready audit export beta onboarding (Splunk HEC)
next_steps: Stonewire to confirm Splunk HEC endpoint URL, token scope, and target index/sourcetype for Redwood audit events
Redwood to enable SIEM export beta feature flag for Stonewire tenant and create initial destination config in staging for a dry run
Stonewire to provide outbound allowlist requirements (if any) / confirm TLS inspection or proxy constraints
Redwood to send Splunk HEC setup guide + recommended SPL queries and dashboards for validation
Schedule weekly 30-min check-in (Tuesdays) for beta feedback, metrics review, and connector health
action_items: Fatima Noor (Redwood) — Send Splunk HEC setup guide + schema v1 link + dedupe guidance by EOD 2025-02-06
Felix Schneider (Redwood) — Enable tenant feature flag + confirm Console UI visibility for Stonewire admins by 2025-02-07
Kevin Osei (Redwood) — Share recommended filtering defaults (admin/security events) and PII/redaction notes by 2025-02-07

summary: Beta onboarding with Stonewire to stand up Redwood’s SIEM-ready audit export to Splunk HEC. The team walked through destination requirements (HEC URL/token/index, optional HEC ACK), filtering strategy to keep noise/cost down, and how at-least-once delivery can produce duplicates. Redwood demo’d the “send test event” flow and aligned on success metrics for the beta: delivery latency (p95), completeness (no missing critical admin/security events), and operational visibility (backlog/last success/last error). Weekly check-in cadence agreed (Tuesdays).
topics: Splunk HEC configuration (token/index/sourcetype, ACK vs no-ACK), destination validation + test event, filtering (event types, actors, env), delivery semantics (at-least-once, dedupe key), metrics for beta success (latency/completeness/error rate), operational workflow (pause/replay), rollout plan (staging → prod).
transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Meeting: Stonewire Software x Redwood — SIEM-ready audit export beta onboarding (Splunk HEC)
Date: 2025-02-06
Time: 17:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes

Attendees
- Fatima Noor (Redwood) — Solutions Engineering (regulated customers)
- Kevin Osei (Redwood) — Security Engineering (SIEM export)
- Felix Schneider (Redwood) — Console / Control plane
- Colin O'Donnell (Redwood) — Beta customer solutions (Private)
- Jordan Lee (Stonewire) — Security Engineering
- Mina Patel (Stonewire) — Platform Engineering
- Avery Chen (Stonewire) — SRE
- Samir Rahman (Stonewire) — Compliance

Auto-summary (generated)
- Goal: Configure Splunk HEC destination, verify test events, align on beta success metrics and check-in cadence.
- Key decisions: Use at-least-once delivery; Stonewire will dedupe on event_id; start with a filtered set of admin/security events; target p95 delivery under ~5 minutes in steady state.

Questions captured
- Do we need Splunk HEC ACK turned on?
- What’s the dedupe key exactly and is it stable across replays?
- Can we separate staging vs production audit streams and indexes?

Action items (captured)
- Redwood to enable feature flag + provide setup docs + recommended SPL queries.
- Stonewire to provide HEC endpoint, token, index, and any network constraints.

---

[00:00] Fatima Noor: Cool. Thanks everyone for joining. This is the beta onboarding for the SIEM-ready audit export. The agenda is basically: confirm your Splunk HEC details, walk through the config in the Console, send a test event, and then agree on what “success” looks like and how we do weekly check-ins.

[00:19] Jordan Lee: Sounds good.

[00:20] Mina Patel: Yep.

[00:22] Fatima Noor: Quick roll call—Fatima, solutions. Kevin is our security lead on the exporter. Felix from Console. Colin is also here in case we touch private deployment stuff, but I think today is mostly hosted/dedicated.

[00:35] Kevin Osei: Hey everyone.

[00:36] Felix Schneider: Hi.

[00:38] Jordan Lee: Jordan, security engineering. Avery is our SRE. Mina platform. Samir compliance.

[00:45] Samir Rahman: Hi.

[00:46] Avery Chen: Hey.

[00:48] Fatima Noor: Great. Before we go into Splunk—can you confirm what you’re trying to detect/monitor with the audit stream? Like top use cases.

[01:00] Jordan Lee: Primary is admin actions in Redwood. Key creation, key rotation, role changes, login attempts, SSO config, basically anything that would be part of an incident timeline.

[01:15] Samir Rahman: And for compliance, we need evidence that changes are logged and we can retain them in our system. We’re not asking you for infinite retention, we’ll retain on our side.

[01:27] Fatima Noor: Makes sense. That matches the beta scope: account/workspace admin and security posture events. We’re not exporting like every single model inference request. It’s audit events.

[01:39] Mina Patel: Right, we don’t want the noisy stuff.

[01:41] Kevin Osei: And just to set expectations—delivery is at-least-once. So you might see duplicates, especially around retries or if you use replay. We’ll give you a stable id to dedupe on.

[01:52] Jordan Lee: Okay.

[01:53] Avery Chen: At-least-once is fine as long as we can dedupe deterministically.

[02:00] Fatima Noor: Yep. We’ll get into that in a sec.

[02:05] Felix Schneider: I’ll share screen in a minute for the Console flow.

[02:08] Fatima Noor: Cool. Jordan, can you share what Splunk HEC setup you have? Like, do you already have an HEC endpoint and token ready?

[02:16] Jordan Lee: We have HEC enabled in our Splunk Cloud. We’ll create a token dedicated to Redwood. We typically set sourcetype like “redwood:audit” or something. Index is “security”.

[02:29] Mina Patel: We also sometimes use HEC ACK if the sender supports it. It helps with confidence on ingestion.

[02:36] Kevin Osei: We do support HEC ACK optionally. It’s not required, but it changes how we treat a successful write. Without ACK, a 200 from HEC is our success. With ACK, we also wait for ackId confirmation.

[02:51] Avery Chen: Does that increase latency a lot?

[02:53] Kevin Osei: It can. It depends on Splunk ack settings and load. Usually it’s a small hit, but if you’re optimizing for lowest latency you might skip it. If you’re optimizing for strongest confirmation semantics, you turn it on.

[03:06] Jordan Lee: For beta, I think we can start without ack and then decide.

[03:10] Mina Patel: +1.

[03:12] Fatima Noor: Great. So minimum we need: HEC endpoint, token, index, and optionally sourcetype. Also confirm TLS—Splunk Cloud is HTTPS obviously.

[03:23] Jordan Lee: Yep. No mutual TLS, just standard.

[03:27] Fatima Noor: Okay.

[03:30] Felix Schneider: Let me share. (pause) Can you all see my screen?

[03:35] Jordan Lee: Yep.

[03:36] Felix Schneider: Cool. In the Console, under Security there’s “Audit Export” — it’s behind a feature flag right now, so if you don’t see it yet in your tenant, that’s expected. Once enabled, you’ll be able to create a destination. Destination type: Splunk, Datadog, or S3. We’ll pick Splunk.

[03:56] Felix Schneider: Fields: name, HEC URL, token, index, sourcetype, batch size, and a toggle for ACK. Plus filters.

[04:08] Mina Patel: Batch size in events or bytes?

[04:11] Felix Schneider: In events. Under the hood we also cap payload size. We’ll default to a conservative batch to stay under HEC limits.

[04:20] Avery Chen: What happens on partial failure? Like one bad event in a batch.

[04:25] Kevin Osei: For Splunk, their response usually indicates success/failure for the request, not per-event. If we get a 4xx schema-ish error, we classify it as non-retryable and we’ll DLQ the batch with details. If it’s 5xx or 429 we retry with backoff.

[04:41] Avery Chen: So DLQ means you store it on your side?

[04:44] Kevin Osei: In the service, yes, there’s a dead-letter queue for poison pills. Operators can inspect and replay after remediation.

[04:52] Samir Rahman: Is there an audit record for changes to the export configuration itself?

[04:57] Kevin Osei: Yes. Changes to destinations—create/update/delete, enable/disable—are themselves audit events. So you’ll see “audit_export.destination.updated” type events in the stream.

[05:10] Samir Rahman: Good.

[05:12] Fatima Noor: Felix, can you show the filters section?

[05:15] Felix Schneider: Yep. Filters are basically include/exclude. In beta we support filtering by event_type, actor, workspace, environment, and time window for replay tooling. For the live stream, you typically set event_type include list.

[05:31] Jordan Lee: We want admin/security only, not like user-level stuff.

[05:35] Kevin Osei: Common starter set is: logins, API key create/delete/rotate, RBAC/role changes, SSO/SAML changes, org/workspace membership changes, and “export config changes.”

[05:49] Mina Patel: Can we filter out read-only events? Like “viewed settings.”

[05:54] Felix Schneider: If they have their own event types, yes. In v1 we’re trying to keep taxonomy coarse enough for SIEM, but we do have a “category” field and event_type strings.

[06:06] Jordan Lee: Okay.

[06:08] Fatima Noor: Before we click save, we need your HEC details. For today, we can do a test in your staging Splunk environment or a dev token.

[06:16] Jordan Lee: I can paste a dev HEC endpoint and token in chat after this call. I don’t want to read it out.

[06:22] Fatima Noor: Perfect.

[06:25] Felix Schneider: There’s also “Send test event” button. It sends a single synthetic audit event with a known event_id and a marker field like test=true.

[06:34] Avery Chen: That’s great. Then we can write a quick SPL query to validate.

[06:38] Kevin Osei: Exactly. And it also validates credentials. If Splunk returns 401/403, we surface it as “auth error” not “transient.”

[06:48] Mina Patel: We’ve had issues with token rotations and permissions. So having that classification helps.

[06:54] Fatima Noor: Yeah we saw that with another customer too—token rotated but the old one remained in some service. We’ll cover rotation in the runbook.

[07:03] Jordan Lee: For Splunk Cloud, tokens are basically all-or-nothing, but we can scope to index.

[07:09] Kevin Osei: Good—least privilege is what we recommend.

[07:12] Felix Schneider: Okay, while we’re waiting for the token, I’ll talk about the health widget. Once enabled, each destination shows state: Enabled, Paused, or Degraded. Degraded means repeated failures and we’re backing off. We show last delivered time, last error, and backlog estimate.

[07:30] Avery Chen: Is there an API endpoint for that too? We might hook it into our monitoring.

[07:35] Felix Schneider: Yes, there’s a health endpoint. For beta, we can share the route and we’ll also have metrics on our side.

[07:41] Fatima Noor: On metrics—let’s align. You mentioned “confidence on ingestion.” Typically we use: delivery latency, completeness, and error rate.

[07:52] Jordan Lee: Right. What can you commit to in beta?

[07:56] Fatima Noor: Beta is best-effort but we want to operationalize it. For success criteria, we usually propose: steady-state p95 end-to-end under 5 minutes; no systematic missing of critical event types; and ability to detect/triage connector issues quickly.

[08:12] Avery Chen: End-to-end means when the event happens in Redwood to when it’s searchable in Splunk?

[08:17] Kevin Osei: Yes, though Splunk indexing latency is partly on their side. We measure “delivered to HEC” time. For your validation, you’ll likely check “searchable in Splunk” which includes their pipeline.

[08:31] Mina Patel: We can split it. We’ll monitor what Splunk says and you monitor delivered.

[08:35] Fatima Noor: Exactly.

[08:37] Samir Rahman: Completeness—how do we prove we didn’t miss anything?

[08:41] Kevin Osei: Great question. In beta, we don’t have full historical backfill for all tenants. But for the live stream, we can provide guidance: use monotonic event timestamps plus request_id correlation. If you suspect gaps, we can run a replay for a time window.

[08:58] Samir Rahman: Replay is like re-sending old events?

[09:01] Kevin Osei: Yes, with safeguards. It’s not “silent.” It will generate duplicates. That’s why dedupe is important.

[09:08] Jordan Lee: What’s the dedupe key?

[09:10] Kevin Osei: In schema v1, there’s an event_id which is globally unique per event. That’s what you dedupe on. There’s also a stable combination (tenant_id, event_id) to be safe across environments.

[09:22] Avery Chen: Is it a UUID?

[09:23] Kevin Osei: Yep, UUID-like.

[09:26] Mina Patel: Can it ever change across replays?

[09:28] Kevin Osei: No, replay is re-delivery of the same stored event. So event_id stays the same.

[09:34] Jordan Lee: Perfect.

[09:36] Felix Schneider: Also, for S3 sink we do object naming for idempotency, but for Splunk it’s really on dedupe logic downstream. Splunk doesn’t dedupe by default.

[09:46] Avery Chen: We can build it in Splunk with a lookup or use a summary index. Or we can tolerate duplicates if they’re low volume.

[09:54] Jordan Lee: For security, duplicates are okay. Missing is not.

[09:58] Fatima Noor: Agreed.

[10:00] Fatima Noor: Let’s talk about filter defaults. Kevin, what’s the minimal set you’d recommend?

[10:05] Kevin Osei: For your use case: authentication events (login.success/login.failed), api_key.created/api_key.rotated/api_key.deleted, rbac.role.assigned/removed, workspace.member.added/removed, and audit_export.destination.* events.

[10:24] Jordan Lee: Good. We might also want “model access policy changed” if that exists.

[10:28] Kevin Osei: There is a policy change event. Sometimes transcription calls it “model allow list” but yeah, it’s part of admin config.

[10:37] Felix Schneider: We can add that to include list.

[10:40] Mina Patel: Does filter support exclude too?

[10:42] Felix Schneider: Yes, include has precedence, then exclude can remove. But we recommend keep it simple: include-only.

[10:52] Fatima Noor: Okay.

[10:54] (crosstalk)

[10:55] Avery Chen: Sorry—one more question: rate limits. If we have like a lot of failed logins, will this backpressure your main API?

[11:03] Kevin Osei: The exporter is isolated. There are explicit backpressure controls so it doesn’t impact inference latency. Worst case, export lags and backlog grows. That’s why we alert on backlog bounds.

[11:16] Avery Chen: Great.

[11:18] Fatima Noor: And for beta we’ll keep an eye on it. If there’s a storm, we might pause the destination.

[11:23] Jordan Lee: Pause meaning stop sending to Splunk?

[11:26] Felix Schneider: Exactly. State machine: enabled/paused/degraded. Paused stops delivery but events continue to be buffered up to retention in the queue. Then you can resume.

[11:38] Jordan Lee: Good.

[11:40] Fatima Noor: Okay. Let’s align on environments. Do you want a separate Splunk index for staging events vs prod?

[11:47] Mina Patel: Ideally yes. We have a “security-dev” index for test. Then “security” for prod.

[11:54] Jordan Lee: And we’ll likely want to start in dev index.

[11:58] Fatima Noor: Great, we’ll do that.

[12:01] Felix Schneider: When you create the destination, you also choose environment: prod or staging. So you can create a staging destination first.

[12:10] Avery Chen: Nice.

[12:12] Fatima Noor: Quick timeline: once we get the token, we can do staging today/tomorrow. Then we can enable prod after you validate queries and parsing.

[12:22] Jordan Lee: Works.

[12:24] Samir Rahman: Parsing—are fields JSON?

[12:27] Kevin Osei: Yes, we send JSON payload. Splunk can parse it. We also recommend setting sourcetype to JSON and doing field extractions. We’ll provide recommended settings.

[12:41] Samir Rahman: Any PII fields?

[12:43] Kevin Osei: We have rules: no plaintext secrets, no full API keys, no prompt contents. Actor identifiers could be email depending on your config. IP address may be included for security events. There’s a redaction policy in the schema doc.

[12:58] Jordan Lee: IP is fine for us.

[13:00] Mina Patel: Email is okay too, we treat it as internal.

[13:04] Fatima Noor: Okay.

[13:06] Felix Schneider: So, we’ll wait for your HEC URL/token after call. Once we have it, we’ll create the destination and use “Send test event.” You’ll search for event_id in Splunk.

[13:18] Avery Chen: We can do a query like index=security-dev sourcetype=redwood:audit test=true.

[13:24] Felix Schneider: Exactly.

[13:26] Fatima Noor: Let’s talk about success metrics more concretely so we’re aligned for the weekly check-in.

[13:31] Jordan Lee: We care about delivery latency and completeness for those critical events. What’s your measurement?

[13:38] Kevin Osei: We track: (1) delivered_count vs attempted_count per destination, (2) end-to-end latency from event time to successful sink delivery, (3) backlog depth, (4) DLQ volume.

[13:52] Avery Chen: Can you share those dashboards?

[13:54] Fatima Noor: We can share screenshots and we can also give you summary numbers in weekly check-ins. For now, dashboards are internal, but we can expose some in the Console health panel.

[14:07] Felix Schneider: The Console health panel will show the basics. We can also export metrics via an endpoint if needed.

[14:14] Mina Patel: For completeness, we’ll do spot checks: trigger known actions and verify they show up.

[14:20] Jordan Lee: Like create an API key, rotate it, change a role, and see those events.

[14:26] Kevin Osei: Exactly. We can provide a validation checklist.

[14:31] Fatima Noor: Let’s propose initial targets for beta:
- Latency: p95 under 5 minutes steady state; p99 under 15 minutes.
- Completeness: For the included event types, no missing events in those “trigger + verify” tests; and in normal ops, success rate >= 99.5% delivered attempts.

[14:57] Avery Chen: 99.5 is okay for beta. For GA, we’d want higher.

[15:02] Fatima Noor: Yep, beta is to learn.

[15:04] Samir Rahman: And we need an escalation path if it starts dropping.

[15:08] Fatima Noor: You’ll have me + on-call SRE. During beta we’ll also have a Slack channel for quick triage.

[15:16] Jordan Lee: Okay.

[15:18] Mina Patel: One more thing: do you support multiple destinations? Like can we send to Splunk and S3 simultaneously.

[15:25] Felix Schneider: In beta, yes, you can create multiple destinations. Each has independent state and checkpointing.

[15:33] Mina Patel: Good.

[15:35] Kevin Osei: Just be aware that filtering is per destination. So you can do high-signal to Splunk and “everything allowed” to S3 if you want, but again beta scope is not everything.

[15:47] Jordan Lee: We’ll stick to Splunk for now.

[15:50] Fatima Noor: Cool.

[16:00] (brief pause)

[16:02] Fatima Noor: On weekly cadence—Tuesdays 10am Pacific work for you?

[16:07] Jordan Lee: I can do that.

[16:08] Avery Chen: Works.

[16:10] Mina Patel: Same.

[16:11] Samir Rahman: I may not attend every week but can join if needed.

[16:15] Fatima Noor: Great, we’ll set a recurring 30 minutes.

[16:18] Felix Schneider: We’ll also capture issues in a shared doc or email recap. Up to you.

[16:23] Jordan Lee: Email recap is fine.

[16:25] Fatima Noor: Okay.

[16:27] Avery Chen: Can we talk about network egress? Do you send from a fixed IP range?

[16:33] Fatima Noor: For hosted, we have a published egress range per region, but it can change. For dedicated, we can do more static depending on setup. Are you IP restricting HEC?

[16:46] Jordan Lee: Not currently, but we might. Splunk Cloud has allowlists.

[16:52] Kevin Osei: In beta, we recommend you avoid strict IP allowlists unless required, because it can cause intermittent blocks if ranges shift. If you need it, we’ll coordinate.

[17:04] Jordan Lee: Okay.

[17:05] Mina Patel: We do have a corporate proxy in some environments, but HEC is direct.

[17:10] Felix Schneider: Good. If TLS inspection is happening, sometimes that breaks cert validation. But Splunk Cloud should be fine.

[17:18] Avery Chen: If we do see 5xx from Splunk, what happens?

[17:22] Kevin Osei: Retry with exponential backoff and jitter. If it persists, destination goes degraded, and we slow down. Backlog grows. We page if it crosses threshold.

[17:34] Avery Chen: And if backlog grows too big?

[17:37] Kevin Osei: We have bounds; if we hit a safety threshold we may pause to protect system stability, then coordinate a replay window.

[17:48] Jordan Lee: Okay.

[18:00] Fatima Noor: Let’s also cover token rotation. In Splunk, when you rotate, you generate a new token. In our Console you can update credentials; that change is audited. After update, we’ll do a test event again.

[18:15] Mina Patel: Nice.

[18:16] Jordan Lee: Does updating token cause downtime?

[18:19] Felix Schneider: There might be a short blip while worker picks up new creds. It’s seconds to a minute. We can do it off-peak.

[18:28] Jordan Lee: Fine.

[18:30] Samir Rahman: Do you store the token encrypted?

[18:33] Kevin Osei: Yes—encrypted at rest, access restricted, and we audit access to secret material in our control plane. For private deployments you can bring your own KMS.

[18:46] Samir Rahman: Great.

[19:00] (crosstalk)

[19:01] Avery Chen: Sorry, on filtering by actor—can we filter to only admin users?

[19:06] Felix Schneider: Not by “role” directly in beta, but you can filter by actor_id or actor_email patterns. Most customers don’t, because you want to see if a non-admin somehow performed an admin action—though ideally that can’t happen.

[19:20] Jordan Lee: Yeah, we probably shouldn’t filter that.

[19:23] Mina Patel: Agree.

[19:26] Fatima Noor: Cool. So we’ll filter by event_type primarily.

[19:30] Kevin Osei: And by environment—staging vs prod.

[19:33] Fatima Noor: Okay.

[19:35] Felix Schneider: One more UI detail: error messages include an error_id you can paste to support. Sometimes the transcript calls it “copy code.”

[19:44] Jordan Lee: Good.

[20:00] Fatima Noor: Okay, I think we’re good. Let’s recap: you’ll send HEC details after, we enable feature flag, create staging destination, send test event, you validate in Splunk, then we move to prod.

[20:15] Jordan Lee: Yep.

[20:16] Avery Chen: And we’ll align on metrics in weekly.

[20:19] Fatima Noor: Exactly.

[20:22] Mina Patel: Can you also send the schema doc? We want to map fields to CIM if possible.

[20:27] Kevin Osei: Yes, we’ll send schema v1 and examples. For CIM mapping, we can suggest fields like src_ip, user, action, outcome. But we’re not doing custom mappings in beta.

[20:41] Mina Patel: Understood.

[20:43] Samir Rahman: And a note on retention: you buffer for how long?

[20:48] Kevin Osei: For the exporter queue, it’s not meant as long-term storage. It’s for durability during transient failures. For the audit log itself, Redwood retains per our audit retention policy. Export is for you to store long-term.

[21:06] Samir Rahman: Okay.

[21:08] Fatima Noor: Any other questions?

[21:12] Jordan Lee: Not now.

[21:13] Avery Chen: Good.

[21:15] Mina Patel: Nope.

[21:16] Fatima Noor: Great. We’ll send recap email with the docs and next steps. Thanks everyone.

[21:23] (end of transcript excerpt — recording continued with scheduling logistics and off-topic Q&A)

Note: Fireflies transcription may omit some scheduling chatter and may contain minor inaccuracies in product names/field labels.
